newsitem.title: USA: KinderCare seen back on growth track.
newsitem.headline: KinderCare seen back on growth track.

text.p: KinderCare Learning Centers Inc, after agreeing to a $600 million buyout deal led by Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co, is better positioned to exploit demographics that promise strong growth for the day-care industry.
Analysts said an influx of capital from the buyout would allow the company to loosen up a conservative growth strategy instituted after new management took over last summer.
James Janesky, an analyst at Stephens Inc, said KKR's offer to pay $20.25 per KinderCare share was fair.
"It is a very attractive valuation for the shareholders. Day-care companies are being valued in the market at five to seven times EBITDA, and this is at seven," he said.
Janesky said KinderCare's new management had brought development of new day-care centers nearly to a halt.

"In the day-care market, when you open up new centers it takes about two years from siting to opening day before a new center starts affecting revenues, and another six to nine months before it starts hitting profitability," he said.
"So the stock price was going to stay at where it was in the 14-15 range unless and until development was accelerated again," he said.
The company produces annual EBITDA of about $90 million, and "the deal was the best bet for shareholders," he said.

He said the building of day-care centers was curtailed because the new management "felt that the ones that were in the pipeline did not meet their profitablity requirements, so they put the brakes on.
The analyst said the overall demographics are very positive for the industry.

"What is happening is baby boomers are having kids, so the growth of the number of children will be sustained and families are having less children per family, so they are willing to spend more per child for day-care," he said.
KinderCare controls 30 percent of the for-profit day-care business, but only about five percent of the overall U.S. market, he said.
